## A Completely Serious Analysis of Extremely Normal Governance

---

So here we are. Another day, another policy announcement that makes you set down your coffee, stare at the wall for a solid forty-five seconds, and quietly ask the houseplant if it's following any of this.

The houseplant, notably, is not doing well. But more on that later.

We are living through what historians will almost certainly describe as "a period," which is the academic way of saying something unprintable. Our current government, a finely tuned machine operating at the peak of whatever this is, has been delivering policy decisions at a pace that can only be described as *enthusiastic* — the way a golden retriever is enthusiastic about running directly into a screen door. The energy is undeniable. The direction is questionable. The screen door is the entire global economy.

But let's be fair. Let's put on our both-sides hats, take a deep breath, and examine what's actually happening with clear eyes and open minds.

Ha. Just kidding. Let's get into it.

---

## **The Economy: Strong, Actually, Please Stop Asking**

The administration recently unveiled what economic advisors are calling a "bold" trade strategy, which is Washington-speak for "we did this without telling anyone, including ourselves." The centerpiece, of course, is tariffs — those wonderful little taxes that somehow surprise everyone except the economists, historians, foreign governments, literally every business owner, and your uncle who took one community college macroeconomics course in 1987 and has been dining out on it ever since.

The logic, as it was explained to us through a series of social media posts written in what appears to be a very caffeinated stream of consciousness, is that if we tax imported goods, foreign countries will be punished, American manufacturing will flourish, and everyone will buy American products because they will have no choice because everything else will cost approximately one mortgage payment.

What actually happened, in the spirit of full disclosure, is that the stock market responded the way a patient responds to unexpected surgery — with immediate, violent rejection. Billions of dollars evaporated from retirement accounts belonging to people who had spent thirty years carefully avoiding financial risk, only to discover that their carefully constructed nest egg was apparently one impulsive weekend Truth Social post away from becoming a carefully constructed nest *minus several eggs*.

But here's where the administration's communication strategy truly shines. When the market dropped, officials explained that this was, in fact, going well. It was a "short-term adjustment." A "detox." The economy, we were told, had been too reliant on other countries, which is a little like telling someone who has driven the same route to work for twenty years that they've been "too reliant on roads."

The solution, apparently, is to negotiate. Which would be a completely reasonable response if the negotiations had been *part of the original plan* rather than the emergency backup plan activated after the first plan detonated in a crowded room.

Small business owners across the country, people who built their companies with genuine grit and creativity, found themselves explaining to customers why prices had gone up, not because of greed, not because of bad planning, but because the materials they needed to make their products now cost considerably more than the products themselves. A furniture maker in Ohio who sources wood fittings from Canada sat down with a reporter and said, with the weary patience of a kindergarten teacher on the last day before summer, "We just need to know what the rules are. Any rules. Consistent ones. We can work with rules."

This is where we are. American business owners are begging for *predictability*, which used to be considered such a baseline expectation of governance that nobody thought to ask for it out loud, the same way you don't specifically request that airplane pilots stay awake during the flight.

---

## **The Environment: A Love Story (For Industry)**

Meanwhile, over in the Department of the Interior, which has been redecorated in what critics are calling "extraction chic," the administration has been rolling back environmental protections with the focused energy of someone finally cleaning out a storage unit.

National monuments have been reduced in size, because apparently the original size was, to use the technical term, too *monumental*. Protected coastal areas have been opened for drilling, because we have apparently reviewed the research on oil spills and determined that pelicans are more resilient than previously documented. The EPA, which stands for Environmental Protection Agency but has recently been operating under what appears to be a more flexible interpretation of all three of those words, has been enthusiastically deregulating emissions standards on the grounds that clean air, while nice, is perhaps a luxury.

"Energy dominance" is the phrase of the moment, and to be fair, there is something genuinely powerful about the imagery. America, dominant in energy. Standing astride the globe, fossil fuels flowing, asserting its will. It's a compelling vision if you don't look too hard at what energy dominance has historically done to the places where the energy actually comes from, which tend to end up resembling the set of a post-apocalyptic film while the profits end up somewhere considerably more scenic.

Coal, we have been repeatedly assured, is coming back. This is wonderful news for the handful of remaining coal workers and moderately confusing news for the energy market, which has been replacing coal with cheaper natural gas and renewables not because of liberal ideology but because of that famously woke concept known as *lower prices*. Energy companies, which are not known for their sentimentality, have been nodding politely at the coal promises while continuing to invest in other sources, because corporations will do many things for government favor but they will not consistently lose money, and you have to respect the commitment.

The administration pulled back from the Paris Climate Agreement again — it's become something of a recurring bit at this point, the international community's version of that friend who keeps announcing they're leaving the group chat but still somehow comments on every photo — on the grounds that the agreement was unfair to American industry. Whether it is unfair is a matter of genuine debate. Whether the alternative of a gradually destabilizing climate is also somewhat inconvenient for American industry is a question that remains, for now, politely unasked in official briefings.

The houseplant mentioned earlier, by the way, is wilting due to unprecedented February heat. It did not take a political position. It simply wilted.

---

## **The Budget: Cutting What Exactly?**

Efficiency has been the watchword of the day, delivered unto us via a newly created apparatus staffed by a collection of extraordinarily wealthy individuals who have volunteered their time to eliminate government waste, which is a little like asking people who've never ridden public transit to redesign the bus system, but let's keep an open mind.

The efficiency initiative has produced some genuinely creative results. Programs that help low-income families pay heating bills have been flagged as inefficient. School lunch funding has been identified as an area of potential streamlining. The National Weather Service, which is the organization that tells you when a tornado is about to remove your house from its foundation, has faced staffing cuts, which meteorologists have described with professional restraint as "a concern," and which people who live in tornado country have described with considerably less professional restraint.

In a particularly inspired move, various scientific research programs have been eliminated or defunded, including studies on infectious disease, cancer treatments, and agricultural resilience — the kind of boring, unglamorous research that tends to be completely invisible until the moment it becomes the only thing standing between civilization and a very bad outcome. This research, we're told, represents government overreach and inefficiency, which is one way to describe it, in the same sense that a smoke detector represents an overreach into the previously unregulated freedom of your kitchen to do whatever it wants.

The cuts, promoters explain, will save enormous amounts of money. Critics note that some of these programs return many dollars in economic and social value for every dollar invested, making their elimination what mathematicians would call "negative efficiency," though the response to this point has been a level of quiet that suggests it has not yet penetrated the relevant decision-making chambers.

Defense spending, by contrast, will increase, because there are apparently threats that justify a larger military but do not justify a functioning weather monitoring system, and the logic of this escapes some people but the important thing is to have confidence.

---

There have been deportations of individuals with no criminal records who have lived in the United States for decades, contributing taxes and children and labor to communities that considered them neighbors. There have been cases that have required subsequent clarification, then further clarification, then statements about how the first clarification was actually correct and the second clarification was clarifying the first clarification, which has produced a kind of clarification singularity from which no clear information can escape.

# THE INVISIBLE HAND WAVING GOODBYE: A Satirical Treatise on the Magnificent Incoherence of Neoliberal Signification

## PART THE FIRST: THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO HAYEK, OR HOW TO WORSHIP AN INVISIBLE THING AND CALL IT SCIENCE

### Chapter I: On the Sacred Semiotics of the Free Market and the Sign Systems That Liberate You Whether You Consent to Liberation or Not

The neoliberal project, in its foundational architectural ambition, constitutes perhaps the most audacious act of *semiotic ventriloquism* in the history of modern political economy. It speaks, with tremendous confidence and no small number of endowed university chairs, in the voice of neutrality — presenting itself not as ideology but as *weather*, not as politics but as *physics*, not as a choice but as the inevitable terminus of human rationality itself.

Consider the primary signifier: **FREEDOM**.

In the neoliberal lexicon, Freedom (capital F, always capital F, the capitalization doing considerable ideological heavy lifting) undergoes a remarkable semantic operation. It is systematically evacuated of its relational content — freedom *from* hunger, freedom *from* domination, freedom *from* the particular tyranny of having nowhere to sleep — and refilled, like a bottle from which the wine has been poured out and replaced with instructions for purchasing wine, with an entirely different substance: freedom *to* transact.

You are free. Magnificently, cosmically, perhaps uncomfortably free. You are free to choose between thirty-seven varieties of breakfast cereal while being unfree to choose healthcare. You are free to express yourself in the marketplace of ideas, provided your ideas come with adequate venture capital backing. You are free, most importantly, to *fail entirely on your own terms*, which is apparently the highest expression of human dignity available to you at this particular historical junction.

Roland Barthes, that insufficiently compensated analyst of bourgeois mythology, would have recognized this operation immediately. The neoliberal sign performs what we might call **the naturalization of the constructed** — the transformation of a highly specific, historically contingent, actively engineered set of power arrangements into the background hum of reality itself. Neoliberalism does not say "we have chosen this." It says "this is what choosing *is*."

This is, semiotically speaking, an extraordinary achievement. It is also, let us be precise, *complete nonsense*.

---

### Chapter II: On Human Capital, or the Remarkable Suggestion That You Are a Small Business and Should Conduct Yourself Accordingly

The human being, in neoliberal discursive production, undergoes a process of ontological restructuring so comprehensive that one must pause to admire its ambition if not its decency. The individual is reconstituted as **Homo Economicus** — a rational actor perpetually engaged in the calculation of costs and benefits, a small corporation wearing a human face, an entrepreneur of the self navigating the permanent market of existence.

This figure, the Homo Economicus, is the protagonist of a very specific and very peculiar story. He (and the gendering here is not incidental; the original model is comprehensively male, comprehensively propertied, and comprehensively unburdened by what economists neutrally term "externalities" such as caregiving, community, or grief) — he makes *optimal decisions*.

He is, in short, fictional.

Not fictional in the way that Don Quixote is fictional, which is to say fictional in the service of profound human truth. He is fictional in the way that a corporate organizational chart is fictional: technically a representation of something, but one that bears such a strained relationship to actual behavior that its primary function is ideological rather than descriptive. When economists discover, again and again, through the accumulated evidence of behavioral research, that people are motivated by fairness, by solidarity, by spite, by love, by what their grandmother told them, by whether they had lunch — the response is not to revise the model. The response is to treat these findings as *charming anomalies* in an otherwise satisfactory fiction.

The notion of **Human Capital** extends this logic into the territory of pure satirical gold. You, reading this, are not a person with a history, a body, a set of relationships that constitute you as a self. You are an *investment portfolio*. Your education is not the transmission of civilizational wisdom or the cultivation of the capacity for democratic participation; it is the acquisition of *skills* that improve your *returns* in the *labor market*. You should think about your intellectual development the way a sensible investor thinks about a diversified portfolio, which is to say you should probably be studying something more practical than philosophy.

(The philosophy department would like to note, with some acidity, that the people who designed this system studied philosophy, and perhaps the lesson is different from the one being taught.)

The performance of this human capital, naturally, becomes a *permanent project*. You must rebrand. Upskill. Pivot. Demonstrate **adaptability** — the neoliberal virtue par excellence, the capacity to enthusiastically reorganize yourself around whatever the market currently requires, the moral achievement of having no stable self that the market cannot reach. The opposite of adaptability is not, as one might suppose, *integrity*. The opposite of adaptability is called **structural unemployment**, and it is your fault.

---

### Chapter III: The Sign of Meritocracy, or the Extraordinary Coincidence That Those Who Designed the Race Are Also Winning It

Among the most load-bearing mythological structures in the neoliberal symbolic order is the concept of **Meritocracy** — the proposition that outcomes reflect desert, that position reflects quality, that the hierarchy is a ranking of excellence rather than an inheritance of advantage wearing a fresh coat of self-congratulation.

The sign MERITOCRACY performs a function of *ideological laundering* of such elegant efficiency that it deserves genuine, if horrified, appreciation. It takes the raw material of structural advantage — the compounding of inherited wealth, the social networks built over generations, the differential quality of educational institutions funded by property taxes thereby ensuring that the wealthy educate their children well precisely because they are wealthy — and it converts this material into the language of *individual achievement*.

The rich are rich because they are excellent. The poor are poor because they have not yet adequately developed their human capital. The system is not broken. You are broken. The system is available to fix you, at market rates, on a payment plan.

Michael Young, who *invented* the word "meritocracy" in 1958 as a *satirical warning*, spent the remainder of his life in a state of Kafkaesque despair as the ruling class adopted his satirical invention as a *sincere self-description*. The satire became the ideology. The critique became the justification. This is, we might note, a level of irony that even the most dedicated poststructuralist would find somewhat on the nose.

The meritocratic sign, furthermore, achieves its most magnificent incoherence when confronted with inheritance — the rather substantial mechanism by which approximately forty percent of all wealth is transmitted across generations with no reference whatsoever to merit, excellence, innovation, or any other virtue the system nominally celebrates. When asked to account for this, the neoliberal symbolic order produces a remarkable improvisation: inheritance is the *reward for the merit of the previous generation*, and taxing it is an attack on *freedom*, and if you find this logic somewhat circular, perhaps you should reconsider your hostility to entrepreneurship.

## A Brief Glossary for Newcomers

**"Law and Order"** - A principle of civilization so fundamental that it demands mandatory minimums for marijuana possession and absolutely zero paperwork for purchasing equipment capable of 400 rounds per minute.

**"Soft on Crime"** - What you call your opponent when they suggest that perhaps the crime rate and the bullet rate might share a passing acquaintance.

**"Government Overreach"** - Requiring ID to purchase a firearm. Not, notably, requiring ID to vote, which is simply "election integrity."

**"Personal Responsibility"** - The solution to gun violence, offered as an alternative to policy, despite being considerably harder to implement and impossible to measure.

**"Too Soon"** - Any time someone mentions gun regulations. Applicable period: approximately forever, renewable after each incident.

## An Exclusive Interview

We sat down with Representative Chad Ironclad (R-District Sponsored by Smith & Wesson) to better understand his worldview.

**Us:** You've called yourself America's toughest law-and-order candidate.

**Ironclad:** Absolutely. I believe in consequences. I believe criminals should face the full weight of justice.

**Us:** You also voted against universal background checks seven times.

**Ironclad:** I'm going to stop you there and mention that Chicago has strict gun laws.

**Us:** We hadn't asked about—

**Ironclad:** Chicago.

## The Nuanced Policy Platform, Illustrated

Consider the conservative approach to two comparable situations:

**Situation A:** Someone sells $20 worth of marijuana.
*Appropriate response:* Mandatory minimum sentencing, permanent criminal record, loss of voting rights, ineligibility for federal housing assistance, extensive documentation.

**Situation B:** Someone purchases a weapon capable of firing 100 rounds per minute.
*Appropriate response:* Please don't make it weird.

The elegance of this framework is that it remains internally consistent if you simply never think about it consecutively.

## The Sacred Texts

Supporters frequently cite the Second Amendment, which was written in 1791 by men whose most advanced personal weapon fired one round every thirty seconds and who, between writings, also owned human beings - a detail we're meant to approach with more historical nuance than the Amendment itself.

"The Founders couldn't have anticipated modern interpretations," gun control advocates suggest about the Second Amendment.

"The Founders' original intent must be followed precisely," the same opponents reply, about the Second Amendment specifically, while proposing the Founders' views on everything else are comfortably outdated.

This is called "originalism," and it is a legal philosophy, not a personality disorder, technically.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Isn't it possible to genuinely support both law enforcement AND gun rights without hypocrisy?**

A: Yes, and many people do so thoughtfully. This article is specifically about the politicians who demand maximum criminal penalties on Monday and then vote to eliminate the laws those penalties enforce on Tuesday. That's a real and specific thing that actually happens, documented in voting records, available publicly, which is what makes it funny and also slightly terrifying.

**Q: Aren't Democrats hypocritical too?**

A: Frequently, yes, and there are several excellent articles about that. This is not one of them. Pointing at someone else when criticized is a technique that works better in kindergarten than governance, though its popularity in both settings remains high.

**Q: Isn't this too complicated for satire?**

A: The senator who spent Tuesday morning demanding "accountability" and Tuesday afternoon blocking accountability legislation would like you to think so.

## EDITORIAL NOTE: ON SATIRE vs. GENUINE CRITICISM

*Because this is worth addressing directly and transparently:*

**What this piece IS:**
- Satire targeting **documented policy positions**, not individuals' personal lives
- Criticism of **specific, verifiable legislative records** — including the 2012-2022 period during which 139 members of Congress publicly denied climate science while receiving documented fossil fuel industry donations (per OpenSecrets data)
- A form of commentary with a **long democratic tradition** (Swift, Twain, Colbert)

**What this piece is NOT:**
- A factual news article
- A claim that every Republican voter personally denies climate science
- A suggestion that all conservatives are identical in their views (notable exceptions: many state-level Republicans have supported carbon pricing, clean energy, etc.)

**Genuine criticism worth separating from satire:**
The actual substantive critique embedded here is this: **When public officials publicly deny scientific consensus while accepting industry funding that incentivizes that denial, that's a legitimate governance concern** — separate from the jokes. The satire is the vehicle; the accountability question is real.

**Where satire gets complicated:**
- It can reinforce tribalism rather than illuminate
- It can be misread as factual by audiences primed to believe it
- It can unfairly flatten a diverse coalition into a single caricature

The most honest satirist acknowledges: **the jokes land because of real documented behavior** — and then asks whether laughter is sufficient response to the underlying problem.

[Assistant Response]
# The Libertarian Pizza Summit: A Family Discovers the Free Market Solution to Combinatorial Mathematics

## *Or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Trust the Invisible Hand to Cut the Pizza*

---

The Hendersons had gathered, as they did every third Sunday, in the kind of chaotic splendor that only a truly ideologically committed family can produce. Uncle Rand — named, his mother would tell anyone within earshot and several people beyond it, after "a very important philosopher, not a politician, well, also a politician, but primarily a philosopher" — had called this particular emergency summit because the pizza had arrived, and with it, as pizza so reliably does, arrived *the fundamental question of human liberty.*

"Before anyone touches anything," Uncle Rand announced, holding both palms outward like a man stopping traffic with the conviction of someone who has never actually stopped traffic, "we need to establish some ground rules about property rights."

The pizza sat in its box, cooling philosophically.

---

## I. The Problem, As Stated by Someone Who Believes Problems Are a Government Conspiracy

The problem was, technically speaking, this:

Four family members. Eight slices of pizza. One slice demonstrably rotten — visibly, olfactorily, and by every empirical measure available to the human sensorium. Two family members, Cousin Petra and young nephew Dashiell, were gluten-free. The table was circular. The chairs numbered seven, which is odd both mathematically and, as Aunt Marguerite kept saying while nobody listened, "spiritually, somehow."

The question: In how many distinct arrangements could the family seat themselves such that (a) nobody sits adjacent to a gluten-eater if they are themselves a gluten-eater, (b) nobody eats the rotten slice, (c) each person eats exactly one slice, and (d) the fundamental sovereignty of the individual is preserved at all costs?

A mathematician would tell you this problem, stated as written, contains several logical inconsistencies — four people at a seven-chaired circular table, with constraints that interact in ways the original question doesn't fully specify — and would require significant clarification before any meaningful calculation could begin.

Uncle Rand would tell you the mathematician is probably on the government payroll.

---

## II. The Libertarian Method of Mathematical Problem-Solving

"First," said Uncle Rand, uncapping a dry-erase marker he had brought specifically for this occasion, approaching the refrigerator door as though it were a whiteboard at the Cato Institute, "we have to ask ourselves: Who *owns* the pizza?"

"The pizza place made it," said his wife, Sandra, who had been hoping to eat before nine o'clock.

"Exactly. And before that, the wheat farmers grew the wheat. And before that, the *land*—"

"Rand, one of the slices has mold on it."

"That mold," said Uncle Rand, with the patience of a man who has been very patient in a very specific way for approximately forty-seven years, "has as much right to exist on that slice as any of us have to exist at this table."

"I'm not eating it," said Dashiell, who was eleven and had already developed the foundational life skill of recognizing when the adults in his vicinity had lost the plot.

"No one is *forcing* you to eat it," Uncle Rand said triumphantly, as though this settled something. "That's the beauty of the system."

The system, as best anyone could determine, involved everybody making individual sovereign choices about pizza simultaneously, without coordination, without acknowledging that the rotten slice existed as a collective problem, and without any mechanism by which gluten-free dietary requirements could be communicated to adjacent seat-holders without constituting "coercive information-sharing."

"If Petra wants to tell people she's gluten-free," Uncle Rand explained, "that's her choice. But we can't *mandate* disclosure. The moment you mandate disclosure, you've lost everything."

"I've lost my appetite," said Aunt Marguerite.

"That's your right," said Uncle Rand approvingly.

---

## III. Solving the Equation, Libertarian-Style

The actual mathematics of the seating arrangement, for those keeping score at home, goes roughly like this:

With four people at a circular table of seven chairs, we first select which four of seven chairs they'll occupy — that's C(7,4) = 35 combinations — then arrange the four people within those chairs, with circular permutations giving us (4-1)! = 6 arrangements per chair selection, yielding 210 base arrangements. Then we apply constraints: the two gluten-free members cannot sit adjacent to each other (reducing valid arrangements), nobody eats the rotten slice (removing it from the available pizza pool, leaving seven slices for four people, which is actually fine numerically), and the gluten-free members must each receive a non-gluten slice, which they will, because all remaining slices except the rotten one are regular pizza slices and the problem as stated doesn't specify that any slice *is* gluten-free, meaning the gluten-free family members simply... don't eat gluten pizza... which is a personal choice about consumption, not a mathematical constraint on the pizza itself, and at this point the problem is doing something peculiar where the circular table with seven seats and four people is creating ghost chairs that haunt the arrangement like the specter of a question that didn't fully think through its own premise.

The answer, a mathematician would cautiously suggest, is somewhere between 72 and 210 valid arrangements, depending on how you interpret adjacency in a circular table with empty chairs between people, which is itself a matter of some legitimate mathematical debate.

The answer, Uncle Rand would tell you, is 1.

"There is exactly one valid arrangement," he said, uncapping a second marker because the first had dried out from being held aloft for eleven minutes. "The arrangement in which each individual, exercising their rational self-interest with full information and zero regulatory interference, naturally gravitates toward the optimal seating position through the operation of spontaneous order."

"What if two people want the same chair?" asked Petra.

"They negotiate."

"What if the negotiation fails?"

"It won't."

"What if it does?"

"It won't, Petra, because rational actors with perfect information and no transaction costs will always—"

"I want the chair by the window," said Dashiell.

"So do I," said Sandra.

There was a pause.

"You two need to negotiate," said Uncle Rand.

---

## IV. The Rotten Slice Problem, or: Negative Externalities Are a Myth Invented by the EPA

Here is where the libertarian approach to pizza mathematics reveals its most elegant flourish, which is also, depending on your perspective, its most catastrophic structural failure:

The rotten slice was, by any reasonable definition, a *negative externality*. Its existence imposed costs — olfactory, gastrointestinal, existential — on pizza-adjacent parties who had not consented to those costs. This is, in fact, one of the foundational justifications for regulatory intervention in markets: that sometimes one bad slice ruins the whole box, metaphorically and also literally, and that "just don't eat it" is insufficient guidance when the bad slice is sitting *right there*, affecting everyone's experience of the pizza ecosystem.

Uncle Rand had a response to this.

"The rotten slice," he said, "is performing a market function. It is signaling to consumers that the pizza provider has failed to maintain quality standards, which means consumers will take their business elsewhere, which means the pizza provider will improve, which means the market has solved the problem without any intervention."

"We already paid for the pizza," said Sandra.

"A lesson about due diligence," said Uncle Rand.

"The pizza is here. In this box. The rotten slice is affecting the smell of the other slices right now."

"That is the smell of freedom."

"It smells like garbage."

"What you're calling garbage," said Uncle Rand, with the serenity of a man who has fully decoupled consequence from ideology, "I call market feedback."

Nobody ate the rotten slice. This was hailed by Uncle Rand as a complete vindication of the system. Nobody pointed out that the system had produced the rotten slice, failed to prevent its inclusion in the box, provided no mechanism for its removal, and that the reason nobody ate it was simply because it was visibly, obviously, aggressively rotten — a fact that required no philosophical framework, only functional eyeballs.

*An op-ed from someone who has definitely thought about this very hard*

---

I'll be honest with you. When I hear the words "universal healthcare," I feel a chill run down my spine — right past the vertebrae I can afford to have examined annually.

The radical proposition that *every American deserves medical treatment* represents perhaps the greatest threat to freedom since the government forced us to stop dumping lead in children's cereal. And I, for one, will not stand for it. Sitting, as my cardiologist recommends, is fine. I see him quarterly.

**The Dignity of Choosing Your Suffering**

Critics claim the current system produces inequitable outcomes — that ZIP code, race, and income predict health outcomes more reliably than, say, personal responsibility. But consider what we'd *lose* if we fixed that.

Character, for one thing.

There is something profoundly *building* about a 34-year-old mother rationing insulin. It teaches her children resilience. It teaches her creditors patience. It teaches her that freedom, true freedom, sometimes means the freedom to experience completely preventable organ failure on a payment plan.

The *market*, that beautiful invisible hand, has already decided what her pancreas is worth. Who are *we* — the government, elected by the people, theoretically serving the people — to second-guess it?

**The Slippery Slope Nobody Is Discussing**

If we guarantee healthcare to everyone, what comes next? Guaranteed *food*? Guaranteed *housing*? Before you know it, Americans will be living in some horrifying Scandinavian hellscape where people are inexplicably happier, live longer, and somehow still manage to develop internationally competitive economies without the motivational threat of medical bankruptcy.

I shudder to imagine it.

**On the Subject of Cost**

Opponents of the current system love to point out that America spends *more* per capita than any universal system while covering fewer people and producing worse outcomes. They call this "evidence." I call it "a lot of numbers said quickly."

Yes, perhaps we spend $13,000 per person annually while Canada spends $6,000 covering everyone. But Canadian healthcare involves *waiting*, and Americans should never have to wait for anything, except in the emergency room, where the average wait is currently 2.5 hours, but that's different because it's alphabetically near "freedom."

**Addressing the "People Are Dying" Argument**

Some bleeding hearts — and I use that term both figuratively and, for the uninsured, occasionally literally — argue that approximately 68,000 Americans die annually from lack of insurance access. They present this as a *problem*.

But here's what they're not asking: Were those people *grateful* for the system they died under? Were they appreciating, in their final moments, that at least their suffering wasn't socialist?

We may never know. They're not available for comment.

**A Personal Note**

I have excellent healthcare. I have mentioned this several times in this piece, not because it's relevant, but because I wanted you to know. I made good choices. I was born to parents who also made good choices, specifically the choice to have money, which I've found is the single most effective health intervention available.

If others would simply make similar choices — choosing, for instance, to not be poor, to not be born with preexisting conditions, to not work jobs that don't offer benefits — they too could enjoy the quiet peace of a man who will never have to choose between medication and rent.

That peace, my friends, is called freedom.

---

*The author requests you do not calculate what his tax increase under universal coverage would actually be, as he has not done this and finds the exercise stressful.*

---

**A straightforward note from the actual writer:** The positions above are satirized because they reflect real logical contradictions worth examining — the gap between "freedom" rhetoric and measurable human outcomes, the correlation between coverage gaps and racial/economic inequality, and the demonstrable cost inefficiency of the current system. Reasonable people debate *implementation* of healthcare reform; the satirical target here is specifically motivated reasoning that treats preventable death as acceptable collateral for ideological consistency.

# "Trickle-Down or Trickle-On? A Grateful Nation's Guide to Getting Wealthy by Watching Rich People"

*An Op-Ed by Someone Who Has Been Patiently Waiting Since 1981*

---

I am pleased to report that after forty-three years of patient, optimistic waiting, the prosperity promised by supply-side economics is nearly here. I can feel it. Any day now.

Senator **fictional composite "Brock Wealthington" (R-Wherever)** unveiled his landmark tax framework last Tuesday, which economists are calling either "bold" or "mathematically impossible," depending on which economists you ask and whether those economists want to keep getting quoted in press releases.

The centerpiece: reducing the top marginal rate from 37% to a more spiritually fulfilling 15%, because Senator Wealthington has determined, through careful study of a cocktail napkin, that wealthy people simply aren't trying hard enough due to taxation. Once liberated from the crushing burden of paying slightly more than a server's effective rate, job creators will presumably create so many jobs that we'll have to import jobs from Canada just to keep up.

"This isn't a tax cut for billionaires," Wealthington clarified, standing in front of a banner reading **TAX CUTS FOR JOB CREATORS** at a fundraiser with a $50,000 per plate entrance fee. "This is a tax cut for *future* billionaires. Everyone here represents someone who *used to* be middle class."

The math, he assures us, is self-explanatory, provided you don't look at it.

---

**THE REVENUE QUESTION**

Critics — bitter, small-minded people who insist on using arithmetic — have noted that eliminating taxes on investment income while maintaining full payroll taxes on wages creates a system where a hedge fund manager pays a lower effective rate than the person who microwaves his lunch. Wealthington addressed this concern directly.

"That's class warfare," he said.

When pressed further, he said it again, louder.

His economic advisor, Dr. Harold Pompington of the Institute for Studies We Already Agreed With Before Conducting, produced a 400-page report demonstrating that the tax cuts will pay for themselves through "growth, dynamism, and the confident energy of freed capital." Page 401 would have explained the specific mechanism, but the printer ran out of paper.

The Congressional Budget Office estimated the plan adds $4.7 trillion to the deficit over ten years. Wealthington called the CBO "frankly very negative" and suggested they try being more optimistic, noting that Ronald Reagan also didn't let math ruin a good afternoon.

"The deficit," he explained patiently, "is actually fine when we do it."

---

**THE TRICKLE EXPLAINED**

You may be wondering how, precisely, tax savings for people earning above $400,000 annually will benefit you, a person who earns considerably less than $400,000 annually. Allow Senator Wealthington to walk you through it.

Step 1: Wealthy person receives tax cut.
Step 2: Wealthy person, overwhelmed with gratitude and surplus capital, invests in expansion.
Step 3: *(Several pages of the economic model are missing here.)*
Step 4: You get a job.

"It's simple," Wealthington says. "Money at the top creates prosperity below. Think of it as a fountain."

Critics prefer the phrase "a drain," but they are, again, very negative people.

The historical record, admittedly, shows some inconsistency. The 1981 tax cuts were followed by a recession. The 2001 and 2003 cuts preceded the largest financial collapse since the Depression. The 2017 cuts produced a brief stock buyback bonanza before a pandemic complicated the controlled experiment. Wealthington attributes these outcomes to insufficient tax cutting, the way a doctor might recommend more of the same medication after the patient develops symptoms.

"We've never really tried full supply-side," he insists, with the conviction of someone who has never checked.

---

**THE INHERITANCE QUESTION**

Perhaps most elegantly, Wealthington's plan permanently eliminates the estate tax, which he calls the "death tax" because "estate tax" doesn't make people angry enough at their own funerals.

"Why should a family be punished simply for building generational wealth?" he asked, to applause from people who have generational wealth.

Currently, the estate tax applies to inheritances above $13.6 million. This means the tax affects approximately 0.2% of estates. Wealthington believes this represents an existential threat to the American Dream — specifically, the dream where you inherit $13.6 million and are frustrated by the paperwork on anything above that.

"Any farmer could die and leave his children with millions," he said, describing a farmer who would be relieved to know he's worth millions.

When journalists asked how many actual farmers are affected by the estate tax, the press secretary said the question was "frankly very agricultural" and ended the briefing.

---

**PAYING FOR IT**

Inevitably someone asks how the nation will pay for these cuts. Wealthington has a sophisticated, multi-part answer.

Part 1: Growth.

That's the whole answer.

When told that independent economists project growth insufficient to cover the revenue loss, Wealthington noted that those economists are part of what he calls the "credentialed establishment," which he defines as people who studied economics, which he considers a significant conflict of interest.

His alternative funding mechanism involves "streamlining efficiency," which, when translated from legislative language into English, means reducing Medicaid, nutritional assistance, and education funding — programs used primarily by people who, statistically, are not attending $50,000-per-plate fundraisers and therefore presumably have less stake in the dinner conversation.

"We're not cutting programs," his spokesperson clarified. "We're right-sizing opportunity."

---

**IN CONCLUSION**

Senator Wealthington's tax vision is, at its core, an expression of profound faith — faith that prosperity flows downward, that the wealthy are productive to the precise degree they are untaxed, and that the rest of us, patient and optimistic, will eventually feel the fountain.

I, for one, remain hopeful.

I have been remaining hopeful since approximately the second Reagan administration, which means I am either a committed optimist or have an alarming tolerance for disappointment. Economists disagree on which.

The check, Wealthington assures us, is in the mail.

It is addressed to a yacht.

But some of it — truly, any day now — is going to trickle down to the rest of us.

---

*The author is a middle-income taxpayer who has been told his patience is good for the economy. He is, by all accounts, an excellent economic unit.*

---

**EDITOR'S NOTE:** *Senator "Brock Wealthington" is a composite satirical figure and does not represent any single individual, though readers may notice a family resemblance to several. The economic projections attributed to him are fictional; the actual supply-side economic record is, unfortunately, not.*

# THE MAGNIFICENT SELF-CORRECTING MARKET: A DEVOTIONAL GUIDE FOR THE ECONOMICALLY ENLIGHTENED

## *Being a Complete Manual for Those Who Have Achieved Consciousness Through the Sacred Study of Marginal Utility*

---

### PREFACE: A NOTE ON METHODOLOGY

The following text has been peer-reviewed by three think tanks, all of whom received funding from industries that benefit directly from its conclusions. We consider this a feature, not a conflict of interest, as the market has determined that their opinions are worth purchasing, which by definition makes those opinions correct. Any suggestion otherwise represents a fundamental misunderstanding of how incentive structures work, which you would know if you had read our previous publication, also funded by the same industries.

---

## CHAPTER ONE: THE MARKET IS ALWAYS RIGHT (EXCEPT WHEN IT ISN'T, IN WHICH CASE IT STILL IS)

The Sacred Market, in its infinite wisdom, allocates resources with a precision that no mere human institution could replicate. This has been demonstrated conclusively by economists at universities whose endowments were built by men who made their fortunes through tariffs, land grants, monopolistic practices, and the occasional creative reinterpretation of property rights as they pertained to other human beings.

The beauty of the market is its self-correcting nature. When markets produce good outcomes, this is evidence of the market working. When markets produce catastrophic outcomes — financial crises, environmental devastation, the concentration of roughly half of global wealth in the net worth of people who own multiple superyachts — this is evidence of *insufficient market*. The prescription is always the same. More market. The market is a doctor who, upon finding that his patient is unwell, recommends larger doses of the medicine the patient has been taking for forty years. The patient, to be fair, has not technically died yet, though a significant portion of his organs have.

It is critical to understand that market failures do not exist. What appears to be a market failure is one of three things:

**A)** Government interference that created perverse incentives upstream of the apparent failure, meaning the failure is actually the government's fault and the market is the solution;

**B)** A temporary inefficiency that the market would have corrected given additional time, and the fact that we "intervened" means we will never know how efficiently things might have resolved themselves, possibly quite beautifully, possibly within the next century or two;

**C)** An outcome you personally dislike, which is a *you problem* and speaks to your insufficient commitment to revealed preference theory.

The 2008 financial crisis, for instance, was caused entirely by government policy encouraging home ownership, and had nothing whatsoever to do with the private financial sector's completely voluntary decision to package fraudulent mortgages into exotic instruments that were then rated as safe by agencies paid by the very banks issuing them. The invisible hand, in this case, was simply pointing at Fannie Mae.

---

## CHAPTER TWO: ON THE SACRED NATURE OF PROPERTY RIGHTS (YOURS, SPECIFICALLY)

Property rights are the foundation of all civilization, freedom, and human flourishing. This is self-evident to anyone who owns property. Those who do not own property may find this argument somewhat less intuitive, which is simply further evidence of their failure to own property.

The historical genesis of current property arrangements is, frankly, not relevant. We operate on the principle that legitimate property derives from voluntary exchange, which derives from a prior distribution of property, which derives from a prior voluntary exchange, and so on, in a chain that we encourage you not to follow too far backward because it tends to terminate in an act of conquest, enclosure, or colonial expropriation that complicates the philosophical picture considerably.

John Locke, our patron saint, argued that one acquires property by "mixing one's labor" with unowned resources. This elegant theory applies perfectly to the current situation, if you are willing to accept that:

1. The resources were unowned at the relevant historical moment (consult your preferred definition of "unowned," which may require creative reinterpretation of Indigenous concepts of land stewardship);
2. The labor mixed with said resources was, in a meaningful philosophical sense, one's own labor, even if it was technically performed by enslaved people or indentured workers who did not receive compensatory shares in the resulting enterprise;
3. The resulting property rights remain valid across generations in perpetuity, but the obligations that may have been incurred during their acquisition do not, because that would be punishing children for the sins of their fathers, which we consider barbaric unless those children are poor, in which case their poverty is simply the consequence of their fathers' poor choices.

The taxation of inherited wealth is therefore theft. The inheritance of wealth is therefore freedom. These positions are consistent.

---

## CHAPTER THREE: INNOVATION, DISRUPTION, AND THE HEROIC ENTREPRENEUR

The entrepreneur is the central figure of our cosmology. He — and it is statistically very often he, which the market has determined is not worth examining — *creates value from nothing*, guided only by his superior perception of consumer desires, his willingness to take risks, and the eight hundred thousand dollars his parents provided as seed capital, which we prefer to describe as "a small loan" in order to emphasize the heroic dimension of his journey.

The entrepreneur's reward — his billions, his fleet of electric vehicles, his space program, his acquisition of social media platforms for the purpose of personal expression — is not merely justified but *necessary*. Without the prospect of becoming the world's first trillionaire, innovation would cease entirely. Human beings would simply stop inventing things, because the historical record clearly shows that no meaningful invention occurred prior to the carried interest tax provision.

Consider what the entrepreneur sacrifices. He works eighty hours a week, which is by all measures an extraordinary commitment, particularly relative to the single parent working three jobs at fifty hours a week each who nonetheless fails to generate comparable value, presumably because she has not disrupted anything. Hard work, as the market understands it, is not measured in hours but in *equity upside*, which explains why a hedge fund manager who golfs on Wednesdays is working harder than a coal miner by any economically rigorous definition.

The entrepreneur also takes *risks*. He risks his capital. He does not, typically, risk his health insurance, his housing stability, his ability to feed his children, or his physical safety, as those risks are more equitably distributed among his workforce, which allows him to focus on the higher-order risk-taking that generates innovation. This is an efficient division of risk-bearing that should not be unionized.

---

## CHAPTER FOUR: A GUIDE TO DISCUSSING POVERTY WITH MAXIMUM THEORETICAL ELEGANCE

Poverty is a complex phenomenon. At its core, poverty represents the revealed preference of individuals who have chosen, through a series of decisions, not to have money. The market does not produce poverty; it simply makes visible the consequences of individual choices, geographic circumstances, historical contingencies, structural disadvantages, inherited trauma, underinvestment in public goods, regressive taxation, wage suppression, and personal moral failures, of which the last item on this list is the only one we consider within the purview of economic analysis.

The poor, it must be understood, *respond to incentives*. This is the cornerstone of our analysis. If you provide them with food, housing, healthcare, or cash, they will have less incentive to not be poor, and will therefore remain poor, possibly permanently, representing a catastrophic misallocation of resources and a moral injury to their characters. The compassionate approach is therefore to ensure they experience the full consequences of poverty, up to and including its most severe expressions, because only through the bracing encounter with destitution will they develop the initiative necessary to — in the words of a famous government minister — *get on their bikes*.

We acknowledge that not all poverty is the result of individual failure. Some poverty results from *structural factors*, by which we mean government policy. The solution to government-created poverty is the removal of government, which will allow the market to create prosperity, which it has consistently done for those positioned to benefit from it, a group that grows more exclusive with each passing decade through a process we decline to characterize as anything other than the natural sorting of talent.

The persistence of intergenerational poverty in the presence of forty years of market liberalization is a data point we are still processing. We expect to have a conclusion shortly. In the meantime, please consult our policy brief, *More Market: An Evidence-Based Approach*, available from our foundation for a suggested donation of $250.

---

## CHAPTER FIVE: REGULATION AND THE VIOLENCE DONE TO FREEDOM

Every regulation is a man with a gun. This is not hyperbole. When the government requires that your pharmaceutical company conduct clinical trials before selling medication to the public, a government agent is pointing a firearm at you. When the EPA suggests that you not discharge mercury into a river, jackbooted thugs are at your door. When health inspectors examine your restaurant's kitchen, you are experiencing something functionally equivalent to totalitarianism, and you are right to say so in your op-ed published in a newspaper owned by a man who benefits from the deregulation you are advocating.

Regulations, unlike markets, are created by fallible humans responding to political incentives. Markets, by contrast,

# BREAKING: Conservative Party Announces Bold New Plan To Make Everything Exactly Like 1987, But More So

*Staff Reporter, The Mostly Fictional Gazette*

---

In what party insiders are calling "our most ambitious forward-looking backward-looking initiative yet," the Conservative Party unveiled a comprehensive 47-point policy platform Thursday promising to fix the nation's problems by identifying which problems existed before 1990 and addressing those instead.

"We've done the analysis," said a spokesperson wearing an aggressively sensible tie, "and it turns out most modern problems are caused by things happening modernly. Our solution is elegant."

---

**TAX POLICY**

The centerpiece involves eliminating taxes on wealth that has been in families long enough to develop its own personality, while introducing a modest new levy on "looking like you're about to ask for something."

Economists estimate this will be revenue-neutral, provided you measure revenue exclusively among people attending the same golf clubs as the economists.

---

**HEALTHCARE**

Rather than expanding coverage, the party proposes making illness "more of a personal responsibility situation." Citizens experiencing expensive medical conditions will receive a strongly worded pamphlet encouraging them to have planned better financially approximately twenty years ago.

"Healthcare is about choices," the platform reads, "and frankly some people are choosing very aggressively."

The proposal also includes defunding seventeen hospital departments while launching a consultation process to study the feasibility of commissioning a report on whether to consider discussing potential reforms, expected to conclude sometime after everyone involved retires.

---

**HOUSING**

Following record housing unaffordability, the party announced a landmark initiative to increase supply by formally requesting that young people "want different things."

"A two-bedroom flat is perfectly adequate if you stop thinking of homeownership as a right," explained a parliamentarian from his fourth property.

The party did acknowledge the housing ladder exists, while proposing to remove the bottom six rungs for efficiency.

---

**ENVIRONMENT**

The environmental platform, titled *"We Also Love The Environment Actually,"* commits to achieving net-zero carbon emissions by 2087, "provided technology figures itself out," and "subject to it not costing anything or inconveniencing the energy sector or requiring behavioral change or frankly coming up again at any future cabinet meeting."

New offshore drilling licenses will be issued "responsibly," defined in the footnotes as "with enthusiasm."

---

**CULTURE AND EDUCATION**

A proposed curriculum reform would replace critical thinking modules with a subject called "Appreciating What We Have," taught alongside mandatory units on why everything was better, discipline-wise.

"Children today are learning too many perspectives," the document warns, "and frankly it shows."

Universities would be required to achieve "viewpoint balance" by hiring at least one professor who thinks the universities have too many professors.

---

**IMMIGRATION**

The party reaffirmed its commitment to reducing net migration to a number that sounds decisive but remains technically undefined, to be enforced through a points-based system awarding credit for skills the economy needs but subtracting points for actually wanting to come here, which is inherently suspicious.

"We value immigration enormously," said the spokesperson, "in the abstract, historically, and in relation to our own grandparents specifically."

---

**THE RESPONSE**

Critics called the platform "breathtaking in its ambition to appear busy while remaining still."

Supporters called it "exactly what this country needs, and also could you keep your voice down."

Party polling shows the platform is popular among voters who describe themselves as "not political" but have strong opinions about everything.

---

## ABSTRACT

This paper undertakes a rigorous, peer-reviewed (by our cats), and comprehensively footnoted examination of the *hypothetical* shortcomings of Extreme Libertarianism — specifically the strain that believes the optimal size of government is "none," that taxation is "literally theft" (as opposed to *figuratively* theft, a distinction we explore at length in Appendix C), and that the free market, left to its own devices, will eventually solve everything including but not limited to: poverty, climate change, the DMV, and that weird noise your radiator makes at 3 a.m.

Our findings suggest, tentatively and with great affection, that *perhaps* — and we stress, *perhaps* — a society composed entirely of sovereign individuals each governing their own micro-nation of one apartment and two cats may encounter certain *logistical difficulties.* We present these findings not with malice but with the warm, weary energy of someone who has attended one too many libertarian meetups and eaten one too many unregulated hot dogs.

**Keywords:** Invisible Hand, Pothole Sovereignty, Voluntary Tax Trauma, The Gary Problem, Soup

---

## 1. INTRODUCTION

Since at least the Enlightenment — and more recently, since someone discovered Ayn Rand in a college dorm and immediately became insufferable at Thanksgiving — political thinkers have grappled with a fundamental question: *How much government is too much government, and at what precise point does "too much government" become "literally any government at all?"*

Extreme Libertarianism, for the uninitiated, is a political philosophy built on the noble premise that individual freedom is the highest social good, that voluntary exchange is the foundation of all civilized interaction, and that if you *really* think about it, stop signs are a form of tyranny.

We at the Journal of Mostly Made-Up Political Science wish to be clear: we respect the intellectual tradition of libertarian thought. Thinkers like John Locke, Friedrich Hayek, and Milton Friedman raised genuinely important questions about liberty, spontaneous order, and the limits of centralized planning. These are serious conversations worth having.

This paper is not about them.

This paper is about the guy at the party who read *Atlas Shrugged* twice and now believes that fire departments should be subscription-based and that he, personally, should not have to pay for a school system because he has "already decided not to have children and frankly finds children exhausting."

This distinction is important, and we ask the reader to hold it firmly in mind like a privately-owned rail pass that may or may not be honored depending on prevailing market conditions.

---

## 2. LITERATURE REVIEW

Previous scholarship on this subject includes:

- **Pompsworth (2019):** *"But Who Will Build the Roads Though, Seriously, Who"* — A landmark study in which the author drove across a hypothetically deregulated highway and aged visibly.

- **Crumble-Hatch & Associates (2021):** *"The Free Market Solution to the Free Market Solution Problem: An Infinite Regress Study"* — Explored what happens when the private company hired to replace government services requires its own regulatory oversight, which must also be private, which also requires oversight, *ad infinitum,* until the entire economy collapses into a recursive nightmare at approximately 4:15 on a Thursday.

- **Johnson, T. (Undated):** A handwritten pamphlet distributed at a gun show entitled *"FREEDOM: A Primer"* — Cited here for completeness and a certain raw enthusiasm.

- **Rand, A. (1957):** *Atlas Shrugged* — A beloved and entirely unironic instruction manual in certain circles, described by its admirers as "the most important book ever written" and by its detractors as "the most important book ever written that also weighs more than a standard house cat."

## 3. METHODOLOGY

Our methodology was as follows:

1. We imagined a society governed entirely by extreme libertarian principles.
2. We watched it unfold in our minds like a slow-motion nature documentary.
3. We took notes.
4. We had a lie down.
5. We had a small glass of wine.
6. We took more notes.

This process was repeated until we had enough material or until the wine ran out, whichever came first. Data collection was entirely voluntary, in keeping with the spirit of the subject matter, which means two of our three research assistants simply declined to participate and we couldn't technically stop them.

## 4. FINDINGS AND ANALYSIS

### 4.1 The Road Problem (Formally Known as "The Gary Problem")

Our first and most immediate finding concerns infrastructure, specifically roads, which arise in approximately **94.7% of all libertarian debates** within the first eight minutes, with a margin of error of ± whatever, we're not statisticians.

In our hypothetical libertarian utopia — which we have named **Garyville**, after a composite archetype we call Gary, who is 34, works in tech, owns precisely one Ayn Rand bookmark, and has strong opinions about helmet laws — all roads are privately owned and toll-funded.

Initial modeling suggested this would lead to efficient, well-maintained roads priced according to market demand. Subsequent modeling revealed the following complications:

- Gary's road is impeccably maintained but costs $47 to traverse, a price Gary considers "fair" and everyone else considers "an act of aggression disguised as economics."
- The competing road, built by Gary's neighbor Dennis, cuts through a wetland because no environmental regulations exist to prevent this, and now there are concerning quantities of frogs in the left lane.
- A third road was proposed but the funding was raised voluntarily, got to 67% of target, and has been "almost done" for six years.

**Finding 4.1:** Roads are complicated. Gary is the worst. Dennis needs to address the frogs.

### 4.2 The Subscription Fire Department Scenario

In our hypothetical, fire departments operate on a subscription model. Citizens pay a monthly fee to ensure their house will be extinguished in the event of fire. This is, proponents argue, a perfectly rational market solution.

We modeled this scenario across 10,000 simulated house fires and found:

- In **62%** of cases, the subscription lapsed because the homeowner "forgot to update their credit card after it was replaced following a data breach at a company whose data security was unregulated because regulating it would have been government overreach."
- In **23%** of cases, the fire department arrived, confirmed the subscription was current, put out the fire, then presented an invoice for "premium flame-intensity surcharge" not mentioned in the base plan.
- In **11%** of cases, a competing fire department arrived simultaneously, leading to a spirited bidding

## CHAPTER ONE: THE INVISIBLE HAND AND OTHER BODY PARTS NOBODY CONSENTED TO

The cornerstone of Bottomsworth's political philosophy is what economists call the "free market" — a concept that functions, in practice, like a dinner party where one guest arrived three hundred years early, ate everything, wrote their name on all the furniture, and now lectures newcomers about the importance of bringing a dish to share.

Bottomsworth explains this with admirable confidence.

"The market *rewards* merit," he told a chamber of commerce breakfast, which is a thing men like Bottomsworth say specifically in rooms where everyone present inherited their starting capital, their connections, their zip code, and in Reginald's particular case, his father's seat on the municipal zoning board.

The feminist critique here is almost too easy, which hasn't stopped us.

Marxist feminist scholar Silvia Federici noted that capitalism required the systematic devaluation of reproductive labor — cooking, caring, raising children — to sustain itself. ## CHAPTER TWO: THE BOTTOMSWORTH BUDGET, ANNOTATED

*The following is excerpted from Reginald P. Bottomsworth's "Common Sense Prosperity Initiative," with critical annotations.*

---

**POLICY 1: "Streamlining Social Support Architecture"**

*What it says:* "We will create efficient, means-tested pathways toward self-sufficiency."

*What it means:* Reducing funding for programs that primarily serve single mothers, disabled people, and elderly women — the demographics who interact most with the state because the state previously helped dismantle the communal and familial structures they relied upon through *earlier* Bottomsworth-adjacent policies.

**Critical note:** Nancy Fraser's concept of the "crisis of care" is useful here. Neoliberal capitalism simultaneously *depends on* care work and *refuses to fund it*, pushing the cost onto individual women while calling this arrangement "personal responsibility." Bottomsworth has called personal responsibility "the bedrock of our values" seventeen times this fiscal year. The bedrock is, notably, not paying anyone's rent.

---

**POLICY 2: "Entrepreneurial Empowerment for Working Families"**

*What it says:* "We believe every family deserves the freedom to build their own future."

*What it means:* Opposing minimum wage increases, paid family leave, and childcare subsidies, while suggesting that the solution to poverty is essentially a better attitude.

**Critical note:** The "empowerment" language here is doing extraordinary heavy lifting. As feminist scholar Angela McRobbie documented, neoliberalism has become remarkably skilled at adopting feminist *vocabulary* — choice, empowerment, independence — while systematically removing the material conditions that make those things possible. 

Bottomsworth loves women. He has *said* so. He said so specifically when opposing the childcare bill, noting that mothers are "the heart of the home," which is a sentence that sounds like a compliment and functions as a policy position that keeps women economically dependent.

**POLICY 3: "Educational Excellence and Parental Rights"**

*What it says:* "Parents, not bureaucrats, should control their children's education."

*What it means:* Defunding public schools while introducing voucher systems that primarily benefit families with existing resources to supplement them, while removing curriculum discussing structural inequality, because — and Bottomsworth has gestured at this without quite saying it — children learning about structural inequality might grow into adults who notice structural inequality, which creates what he calls "division."

**Critical note:** bell hooks argued that education is inherently political — that the question was never *whether* education reflects a worldview, but *whose* worldview it reflects. The current worldview reflected in Bottomsworth's preferred curriculum is one where the market is natural, hierarchies are meritocratic, and the people who wrote the curriculum are the people who should keep writing it.

This is called "neutrality."

## CHAPTER THREE: THE BODY POLITIC, OR, WHAT BOTTOMSWORTH THINKS ABOUT WOMEN'S BODIES (A COMPREHENSIVE REVIEW)

- Housing assistance for single parents

This is not a contradiction, Bottomsworth explains. It is a *nuance*.

## CHAPTER FOUR: ON THE EFFICIENCY OF SUFFERING, OR, WHY EVERYTHING IS ACTUALLY WOMEN'S FAULT IF YOU SQUINT

A recurring theme in Bottomsworth's public addresses is what we will call **the Productivity Tautology**:

1. The free market rewards productivity
2. Productive people succeed
3. Therefore, people who have not succeeded are not productive enough
4. Therefore, assistance programs *create* the problem by *reducing* the incentive to be more productive
5. Therefore, the compassionate choice is to remove assistance
6. *(The condition of people who had assistance removed is not tracked past the press release)*

Patricia Hill Collins' matrix of domination framework is instructive here. Systems of race, class, and gender oppression don't operate in isolation — they intersect and *mutually reinforce* one another. A single Black mother navigating Bottomsworth's "streamlined" benefits system isn't experiencing one obstacle; she's experiencing the compounded architecture of multiple systems designed, at various historical points, with her specifically in mind — as someone to exclude.

Bottomsworth would describe this as "complex."

# Senator Buck Strongjaw's "Patriot Math" Budget Plan Will Definitely Save America (Trust The Numbers)

*By Our Political Correspondent Who Took Eighth Grade Algebra*

---

WASHINGTON — In a bold demonstration that a calculator can be used for both genius and crimes against humanity simultaneously, Senator Buck Strongjaw (R-Somewhere Flat) unveiled his landmark **"Freedom Arithmetic Budget Reconciliation and Eagle Act"** Tuesday, promising it would "make the numbers great again."

The plan is elegant in its simplicity, according to Senator Strongjaw and Senator Strongjaw alone.

**Step One:** Add $500 million to the military budget, because the Air Force apparently needs a seventh golden toilet seat for the administrative wing, and frankly, who among us would argue against that.

**Step Two:** Subtract $200 million from education, because, and we're quoting directly from the Senator's press release here, "children who are TOO educated start asking questions, which is frankly un-American and also personally inconvenient."

**Step Three:** Multiply the resulting difference by two to calculate what Strongjaw's office is calling the "true cost" of the proposal — a figure that his communications director described as "the most important number in the document" and that his budget director described, privately, as "something Buck invented in the Uber on the way over."

The resulting number, $600 million, apparently represents something. Nobody in the Senator's office could agree on precisely what.

"It's the *true* cost," reiterated spokesperson Tiffany Blondell, when pressed for clarification.

"True cost of what?" this reporter asked.

"Of the proposal," she said.

"But the proposal *is* the numbers. So you multiplied the proposal by itself to get the cost of the proposal?"

Ms. Blondell excused herself to take an urgent call that appeared to involve no phone.

---

## Economists React

Dr. Patricia Nguyen, chair of fiscal policy at Georgetown University, reviewed the plan and provided the following statement:

"I have reviewed this budget framework thoroughly and I would like to note, for the record, that multiplying a budget difference by two does not produce a 'true cost.' It produces a different, larger number. These are related concepts but they are not the same concept. I cannot stress this enough. Please help."

Dr. Nguyen then stared at a wall for several minutes.

The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office released a statement calling the methodology "novel," which, in CBO language, translates roughly to "we found this in the parking lot."

Meanwhile, economists at the Heritage Foundation called the plan "bold, visionary, and we will explain why the math works once someone explains to us why the math works."

---

## What The Military Gets

The additional $500 million in military funding, per the proposal's 847-page appendix, is earmarked for:

- **$200 million** — New fighter jets (to complement the existing fighter jets, which were purchased to complement the previous fighter jets)
- **$180 million** — A study on whether the previous studies about fighter jets were conducted correctly
- **$80 million** — "Morale infrastructure," which sources confirm means a Chili's on every aircraft carrier
- **$40 million** — Miscellaneous freedom

Senator Strongjaw appeared emotional during the announcement, placing his hand over his heart and staring toward a flag so long that an aide eventually redirected him toward the podium.

"The men and women of our armed forces deserve the best," the Senator said, to applause from defense contractors who had, notably, pre-printed their applause signs before the speech began.

---

## What The Children Lose

The $200 million cut to education will be distributed, or rather *un-distributed*, across several key programs:

- **$75 million** cut from Title I funding for low-income schools, because poverty "builds character," according to people who have not experienced poverty
- **$60 million** cut from school lunch programs, because hungry children are "more motivated," according to a philosophy the Senator reportedly developed after skipping breakfast one morning and feeling "extremely alert"
- **$40 million** cut from special education services, described in the budget document as "trimming the administrative fat," in a sentence that should haunt everyone who wrote it
- **$25 million** cut from civics education specifically, which, upon reflection, begins to explain the multiplying-by-two thing

When asked about the education cuts at a press conference, Senator Strongjaw explained that he himself attended public school and "turned out fine," gesturing broadly to himself as evidence, inadvertently making several journalists reconsider their priors about public education funding.

---

## The Multiplication Explained

Perhaps the most creative element of the proposal remains the "times two" provision, which the Senator's budget team has described variously as:

- "Standard accounting practice" (it is not)
- "A conservative principle" (it is a number)
- "Something we saw in a spreadsheet once" (most likely)
- "Not up for discussion" (correct, apparently)

When a reporter from the *Financial Times* asked during the Q&A whether multiplying a budget figure by an arbitrary integer is "how budgets work," the Senator replied that the reporter was "clearly a socialist," which is not a rebuttal but did change the subject effectively.

Senator Strongjaw's chief economic advisor, a man named Brad who described his background as "business, mostly vibes," explained that the multiplication accounts for "hidden costs, second-order effects, and the price of freedom, which as everyone knows, is not free, and based on our modeling, costs approximately twice whatever number you started with."

Brad could not be reached for follow-up comment as he was at a conference in Scottsdale.

"Who decided that?" he added, genuinely.

A local schoolteacher, who asked to remain anonymous because she still works in a school that depends on federal funding, noted quietly that $200 million cuts to education tend to "show up in classrooms," specifically in the form of thirty-five students sharing eight textbooks, a situation she described as "fine, apparently, from a policy perspective, since we're doing it."

She then returned to a classroom in which thirty-five students were sharing eight textbooks.

## The Senator Responds To Critics

At a follow-up press event, Senator Strongjaw addressed mounting criticism of his mathematical framework with characteristic directness.

"The radical left wants you to think arithmetic is complicated," he said, visibly comfortable. "It's not. You add the strength. You subtract the weakness. You multiply by two because America does everything bigger. That's in the Constitution, I believe in the back."

*(It is not in the Constitution.)*

"Will this hurt children?" a reporter asked.

"It will make children **stronger**," the Senator replied, in the tone of a man who has never explained this to a child.

"Will it actually cost $600 million?"

The number was $600 million.

It remains unclear what it means.

The bill is expected to pass committee along party lines, be celebrated as a triumph of fiscal conservatism, be implemented in a way that mostly affects people who did not vote for it, and be referenced two years from now in a fundraising email as proof that Senator Strongjaw is "fighting for you," with "you" doing considerable definitional work in that sentence.

Senator Strongjaw is up for reelection in November. His opponent, a former math teacher, is polling at four points behind him.

We are all fine.

- Adapting to climate change by "just moving stuff"

- Three "once-in-a-century" floods in eight years
